props.sub: four more behavioral questions · with full worked answers · Senior EM

props.title: Taking over a new or struggling team
props.q: How do you approach your first 90 days with a new team?

moves.title: Listen before you change
moves.desc: Resist reorganizing on day one. Diagnose first — earn the right to lead.

moves.title: Meet everyone, read everything
moves.desc: One-on-ones with the whole team and key partners; learn the system and the history.

moves.title: Find and ship an early win
moves.desc: Pick one visible, real problem and fix it fast, to build trust and momentum.

moves.title: Then set direction with them
moves.desc: Only once you understand it, set a clear direction the team helped shape.

props.trap: You came in as the “hero fixer” and reorganized everything before you understood it.
props.signal: You lead with humility and diagnosis, then act — you don't impose before you understand.
props.foot: The first 90 days are for listening and one early win — not a grand reorg you'll regret.

props.title: Taking over a team that had lost the company's trust
props.situation: I was asked to take over a team with a terrible reputation. It had missed three launches in a row, other teams had stopped depending on it, and morale was rock bottom. Leadership wanted a fast turnaround.
props.task: My mandate: turn it around — but I resisted the pressure to slash and reorganize on day one.

actions.d: Listened first, for three weeks — one-on-ones with every engineer and every frustrated partner team, just asking what was really wrong.
Found the real problem — it wasn't the people. It was impossible scope, no clear priorities, and constant thrash from above.
Shipped a fast, visible win — I renegotiated scope, cut the roadmap in half, and we delivered one solid thing in a month.
Then set direction with them — a focused mission the team helped write, and I shielded them from the thrash.

props.learning: Resist the hero-fixer urge. Diagnose first, ship one early win, then set direction together.
props.foot: You led with humility and a fast win, not a reorg. That's how you earn a team, not command it.

props.title: Partnering, and clashing, with Product
props.q: Tell me about a conflict with a product manager or partner.

moves.title: Assume a shared goal
moves.desc: You and the PM both want a great product. Start from the goal, not the turf.

moves.title: Separate the what from the how
moves.desc: PM owns the what and why; you own the how and its cost. Respect the line.

moves.title: Bring data and options, not a veto
moves.desc: “No” becomes “here's the cost, and two paths.” Make the trade-off shared.

moves.title: Protect the relationship
moves.desc: You'll work with this person for years. Win the decision, keep the partnership.

props.trap: You made it engineering versus product, or you silently complied and resented it.
props.signal: You're a true partner to product — candid, data-driven, and durable across disagreements.
props.foot: The EM–PM relationship is a marriage. Disagree on the decision; never damage the partnership.

props.title: The PM who wanted it all shipped by Friday
props.situation: My product partner wanted a major feature shipped in two weeks to hit a launch event. My team was certain it needed four — and doing it in two meant cutting testing on a payments flow. It got tense fast.
props.task: My mandate: protect quality and the relationship, without just stonewalling with a “no.”

actions.d: Anchored on the shared goal — we both wanted a successful launch, not a demo that broke live on stage.
Respected the line — I acknowledged the launch date was his call; the engineering risk was mine to make visible.
Brought options, not a veto — I showed the real risk, and offered a phased plan: a solid core at the event, the rest a week later.
Made the trade-off jointly — we chose the phased plan together, and I put it in writing as a shared decision.

props.learning: Turn a “versus” into a shared trade-off. Win the decision with data, and keep the partner.
props.foot: You disagreed hard on the how and still strengthened the partnership. That's the maturity they want.

props.title: Mentoring and sponsoring others
props.q: Tell me about someone you mentored or sponsored.

moves.title: Know the difference
moves.desc: Mentoring is advice you give them. Sponsorship is advocacy when they're not in the room.

moves.title: Invest beyond your reports
moves.desc: The best mentoring often crosses team lines and levels — not just your org chart.

moves.title: Sponsor with your capital
moves.desc: Put their name forward, hand them visible work, and defend it where it matters.

moves.title: Measure it by their trajectory
moves.desc: Did they get promoted, unstuck, or braver? Their growth is the receipt.

props.trap: You described giving generic advice, with no real risk or advocacy on your part.
props.signal: You actively grow people and spend your own credibility to lift them — a force multiplier.
props.foot: Mentoring is talking. Sponsorship is spending your own capital to open a door. Great leaders do both.

props.title: Sponsoring an engineer everyone had overlooked
props.situation: A quiet, mid-level engineer on a neighboring team, Meera, did consistently excellent work but got no recognition. She wasn't loud, she was on a low-visibility team, and she'd been stuck at the same level for years.
props.task: She wasn't even my report, but her own manager wasn't advocating for her — so I decided to sponsor her.

actions.d: Started with mentoring — regular sessions on scope, visibility, and how to navigate the promotion process.
Then actually sponsored her — I pulled her onto a high-visibility cross-team project that I could influence.
Spent my own capital — I put her name forward in staffing rooms, and vouched for her in the promotion calibration.
Coached her manager too — so the advocacy would keep going after I stepped back.

props.learning: Mentoring is advice. Sponsorship is spending your credibility to open a door someone has earned.
props.foot: You spent your own capital to lift someone, with no upside for you. That's the leader they want.

props.title: Getting hard feedback — and changing
props.q: Tell me about tough feedback you received, and what you did.

moves.title: Pick feedback that stung
moves.desc: A real criticism of you as a leader — not “I take on too much.”

moves.title: Own it without defending
moves.desc: The tell is your first reaction: did you get curious, or defensive?

moves.title: Make a visible change
moves.desc: A concrete behavior you altered, that other people could actually see.

moves.title: Close the loop
moves.desc: Go back to the person who gave the feedback and show them it landed.

props.trap: You picked flattering feedback, or you explained why the feedback was actually wrong.
props.signal: You're coachable — you can hear a hard truth about yourself and genuinely change.
props.foot: How you take feedback is how they predict you'll grow. Coachability is a senior-leadership signal.

props.title: The feedback that I was intimidating my own team
props.situation: In a skip-level review, my manager told me something that stung. My team found me intimidating in technical discussions. As a strong engineer, I'd jump in with the answer — and people had started staying quiet and deferring to me instead of thinking.
props.task: My mandate to myself: actually change this, rather than explain it away.

actions.d: Sat with the discomfort — my first instinct was to defend myself, but I made myself get curious and ask for specifics.
Made a visible behavior change — I stopped giving my opinion first in design reviews, and started asking questions instead.
Created space on purpose — I had others present and decide, and I deliberately let the silences sit.
Closed the loop — months later, I asked the team, and my manager, whether it had changed. It had.

props.learning: How you receive hard feedback about yourself is the truest measure of whether you'll grow.
props.foot: You heard a painful truth, changed a real behavior, and checked that it landed. That's coachability.

items: In a new role, listen and ship one win before you reorganize.
Turn product conflict into a shared trade-off, not a turf war.
Sponsorship is spending your capital, not just giving advice.
Coachability — hearing hard feedback and changing — is senior.
Same spine every time: STAR, plus what you learned.
props.closer: The best leaders listen hard, lift others, and never stop being coachable.
